entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of a school building with different rooms labelled in the local language.
2. Ask 'What places do you see in school?' and invite students to point and say in Malay.
3. Introduce the English words for three places: canteen, library, hall, saying each slowly and having students repeat chorally.

 

Lesson Development

Vocabulary Introduction

1. Display flashcards of canteen, library, and hall one by one, each with a clear image and the word.
2. Say each word clearly, emphasizing the sounds (e.g., can-TEEN, LI-bra-ry, hall), and have the class repeat after you.
3. For each word, ask a simple question like 'Do you eat in the library?' to check understanding, and correct with a nod or headshake.

 

Guided Pair Speaking – 'I go to the...'

1. Model the sentence frame: 'I go to the [place] to [activity].' For example, 'I go to the canteen to eat.'
2. Write on the board: 'I go to the _____ to _____ .' and provide a word bank: canteen/eat, library/read, hall/play.
3. In pairs (e.g., DHARSHAYANI with MOHAMAD RYYAN), students take turns completing the sentence orally. The teacher circulates and helps weaker pairs.
4. After 5 minutes, ask a few pairs to share their sentences with the class, praising correct pronunciation and effort.

 

Matching Game – Place & Action

1. Prepare three large cards with place names and three with activities (eat, read, play).
2. Call up two students (e.g., MOHAMAD WAFY HAU and MUHAMAD HARITH AQASHA) to match a place with an activity, then say the full sentence: 'I go to the [place] to [activity].'
3. Repeat with different pairs until all students have had a turn, providing support as needed.

 

Post-lesson

1. Quick recap: Point to each flashcard and ask 'What is this?' – students shout the word.
2. Distribute a worksheet with three pictures (canteen, library, hall) and blanks for a sentence. Students choose one place and write 'I go to the ______ to ______.' using the word bank.
3. Collect worksheets as exit tickets to assess understanding.
entries.reflection_html: Most students could repeat the vocabulary with support, but DHARSHAYANI and MOHAMAD RYYAN struggled with pronunciation of 'library' - they will need extra drilling next lesson. MUHAMMAD NAZRIN and MUHAMMAD THAQIF DANIAL confidently produced full sentences during pair work, showing good progress.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show flashcards of school places (library, field, classroom, canteen) and ask "What place is this?" for choral repetition.
2. Say "I see a library. I see a field. What do you see?" and have students point to the correct flashcard.
3. Sing a simple song: "We go to school, we read in the library, we play on the field, we eat in the canteen" with actions.

 

Lesson Development

Reading Aloud

1. Write on board a short passage: "This is my school. I go to the library. I read books. I go to the field. I play football. I go to the canteen. I eat noodles."
2. Read the passage aloud slowly, pointing to each word, and have students repeat each sentence chorally.
3. Highlight key words: library, field, canteen, and ask students to say them again.

 

Comprehension Questions

1. Give each student a worksheet with three questions: "Where do I read books?" "Where do I play football?" "Where do I eat noodles?" with sentence frames like "I read books in the _____".
2. Read each question aloud, then guide students to find the answer in the passage and fill the blanks using choral repetition.
3. Call students individually (e.g., Dharshanayani, Mohamad Ryyan) to read their completed sentences for the class.

 

Vocabulary Reinforcement

1. On the board, list three places: library, field, canteen. Draw simple icons (book, ball, food) next to each.
2. Say sentences like "I borrow books from the ____" and have students guess the place, then say full sentence chorally.
3. Repeat with "I play on the ____" and "I eat in the ____".

 

Matching Game

1. Prepare a worksheet with pictures of library, field, canteen on the left and sentences on the right (e.g., "I read here." "I play here." "I eat here.").
2. Read each sentence aloud, and have students draw a line from the sentence to the correct picture.
3. Check answers together by calling out sentences and having students point to the picture.

 

Post-lesson

1. Recap: "What did we learn today? We read about places in school. What are the places?" (library, field, canteen).
2. Exit ticket: Give each student a small paper and ask them to draw one place from the passage and write its name with help if needed.
entries.reflection_html: Today, Muhamad Nazrin confidently read the passage aloud and answered questions correctly. Mohamad Wafy Hau struggled with the word 'canteen' but improved after choral repetition. Next time, I will add more picture support for weaker students like Muhammad Syahir Haikal.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher shows pictures of places in school (library, field, canteen, classroom) and asks 'What place is this?' while pointing.
2. Students chorally repeat the names of each place after teacher.
3. Teacher asks 'Which place do you like?' and calls on a few students (e.g., DHARSHAYANI, MOHAMAD RYYAN) to answer using 'I like...'.

 

Lesson Development

Sentence Frame for Favourite Place

1. Teacher writes on board: 'My favourite place in school is the _______.' and explains each word.
2. Teacher models example: 'My favourite place in school is the library.' and asks students to repeat.
3. Teacher shows two more examples: 'My favourite place in school is the field.' and 'My favourite place in school is the canteen.' with choral repetition.

 

Guided Writing with Word Bank

1. Teacher distributes a worksheet with the sentence frame 'My favourite place in school is the _______.' and a word bank of places (library, field, canteen, classroom, hall).
2. Teacher guides students to choose one place and write the sentence on their worksheet, circulating to help weaker students like MUHAMAD HARITH AQASHA and MUHAMMAD AFIQ ZIYAD.
3. Teacher asks students to draw a simple picture of their favourite place next to the sentence.

 

Pair Sharing

1. Teacher pairs students (e.g., MUHAMMAD IZZUDIN with MUHAMMAD NAZRIN) and asks them to read their sentence to their partner.
2. Teacher calls on three pairs to share aloud with the class (e.g., MOHAMAD WAFY HAU, MUHAMMAD SYAHIR HAIKAL, MUHAMMAD THAQIF DANIAL).
3. Teacher praises effort and corrects pronunciation gently.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher collects worksheets for assessment.
2. Teacher asks students to chant 'My favourite place in school is the...' and points to pictures, eliciting each place.
entries.reflection_html: Most students successfully wrote the sentence frame with support from the word bank. MUHAMMAD FIRDAUS ALFANDI needed help holding the pencil, but with guidance he wrote the word 'field'. All students enjoyed drawing their favourite place.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of a clock with activities around it (e.g., wake up, brush teeth) and ask 'What do you do every day?' to elicit prior knowledge.
2. Write student responses on the board, highlighting time expressions like 'at 7 o'clock' and 'in the morning'.
3. Play a short video clip of a person's daily routine (no audio) and ask students to guess the verbs and times shown.

 

Lesson Development

Vocabulary and Time Expressions

1. Introduce key daily routine verbs: wake up, get up, have breakfast, go to school, have lunch, do homework, have dinner, watch TV, go to bed.
2. Present time expressions: at + specific time (e.g., at 7:00), in the morning/afternoon/evening, at night, before/after + activity.
3. Model sentences using the vocabulary and ask students to repeat: 'I wake up at 6:30 in the morning.'

 

Pair Interview: My Daily Routine

1. In pairs (students A and B), each student writes down their own daily routine using the target vocabulary and time expressions.
2. Student A interviews Student B using questions like 'What time do you wake up?' and 'What do you do after school?'
3. Student B answers in full sentences, and Student A takes notes. Then they switch roles.
4. After both interviews, each student shares one interesting fact about their partner's routine with the class.

 

Group Guessing Game

1. Divide the class into groups of 3-4 (e.g., group includes Chai Zi Jian, Huzaifah, and Celine).
2. Each group receives a set of cards with daily routine verbs (e.g., 'have dinner', 'go to bed') and time expression cards (e.g., 'at 8:00 pm', 'in the evening').
3. One student picks a verb card and a time card, then acts it out silently while others guess the sentence: 'You are having dinner at 8:00 pm.'
4. Rotate roles until all members have acted and guessed. The group with the most correct sentences wins.

 

Post-lesson

1. Ask three students to volunteer and share their partner's routine in front of the class, using connectors like 'and then', 'after that'.
2. Conduct a quick error correction on common mistakes (e.g., 'I go to bed at 10 o'clock' vs 'I go to bed 10 o'clock').
entries.reflection_html: Today's speaking activities engaged stronger students like Deni and Jayamitthra deeper in pair interviews, while Keerthikan and Dhiviniesh improved their use of time expressions. The group guessing game fostered teamwork and confidence in speaking. Overall, the class demonstrated good fluency, but some students like Huzaifah need more practice with 'at' vs 'in' for time.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher writes 'My Daily Routine' on the board and asks students to brainstorm daily activities they know in English (e.g., wake up, brush teeth, have breakfast).
2. Teacher elicits a few activities from Huzaifah and Celine to activate prior knowledge.
3. Teacher introduces the goal: to read a routine and then describe our own using linking words.

 

Lesson Development

Reading a Model Routine

1. Teacher distributes a short passage titled 'A Day in My Life' written by a student named Adzin Danish (e.g., 'I wake up at 6 a.m. Then I brush my teeth. After that, I have breakfast. Next, I go to school. I study until 1 p.m. Finally, I go home.').
2. Teacher highlights the connectors 'Then', 'After that', 'Next', 'Finally' on the board and explains they help show sequence.

 

Speaking Chain: My Daily Routine

1. Students read the passage silently for 2 minutes.
2. In pairs (e.g., Ainnur and Deni), students take turns describing their own daily routine to each other, using at least three connectors from the list.
3. Teacher organizes a speaking chain: starting with Kalvin, each student adds one sentence about their routine, using a connector to link to the previous sentence.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher asks a few students to share what connectors they used and how they helped make their routine clear (e.g., Keerthikan shares his sentences).
2. For homework, students write a short paragraph of 5-7 sentences about their own daily routine, using at least four different connectors.
entries.reflection_html: During the lesson, Adzin Danish's passage served as a clear model of using connectors in a sequence. In the speaking chain, Celine used 'then' and 'after that' smoothly, while Deni needed a little prompting to add 'finally'. Overall, students demonstrated understanding of sequence connectors and were able to apply them in describing their own routines.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a short video (30 seconds) of a student's daily routine without audio, and ask students to guess the activities.
2. Elicit daily routine verbs (wake up, eat breakfast, go to school) and write them on the board as a word bank.
3. Say: 'Now we will write about a friend's routine. First, let's see an example.'

 

Lesson Development

Model Paragraph

1. Display a model paragraph on the board: 'My friend Adzin wakes up at 6 a.m. First, he brushes his teeth. Then, he eats breakfast. After that, he goes to school. Finally, he does his homework in the evening.'
2. Underline connectors: 'First', 'Then', 'After that', 'Finally'. Explain they link steps in order.
3. Ask students to identify the subject pronouns (he) and possessive adjectives (his) used for one person.

 

Pair Interview and Write

1. Pair up students: e.g., Ainnur with Celine, Dhiviniesh with Jayamitthra, etc. Each student interviews their partner about their daily routine using questions like 'What time do you wake up?' and 'What do you do after school?'
2. Students take notes on a provided worksheet with guiding questions (wake up, breakfast, school, after school, evening).
3. Individually, each student writes a short paragraph (5-6 sentences) about their partner's routine using the model and connectors. Encourage adding one extra detail (e.g., 'He likes to read before bed.').
4. Teacher circulates to support weaker students (e.g., Deni, Huzaifah) with sentence starters.

 

Post-lesson

1. Choose two volunteers (e.g., Kalvin and Keerthikan) to read their paragraphs aloud to the class.
2. Peer feedback: Partners swap paragraphs and check for correct use of connectors and pronouns using a simple checklist.
3. Collect paragraphs for assessment.
entries.reflection_html: Most students successfully wrote coherent paragraphs with connectors. Adzin and Celine demonstrated strong use of time order words, while Jayamitthra needed minimal support with pronouns. A few students like Deni and Huzaifah required scaffolding but improved with sentence starters.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a slide with 10 hobby images (e.g., reading, cycling, gaming) and ask students to name them in English as a quick recall.
2. Elicit one or two less common hobbies (e.g., origami, calligraphy) to extend vocabulary.
3. Ask: 'How many of you play video games?' and do a quick show of hands to model a survey question.

 

Lesson Development

Hobby Vocabulary & Survey Language

1. Distribute a handout with 20 hobby words (e.g., swimming, baking, photography, skateboarding) and provide simple definitions where needed.
2. Model key survey phrases: 'What is your favourite hobby?', 'Which hobbies do you do in your free time?', 'How often do you...?'
3. Introduce the tally chart template: columns for hobby name, tally marks, and total.

 

Class Hobby Survey & Presentation

1. In pairs (A and B), students take turns asking each other about their hobbies using the modelled questions and record answers with tally marks on the handout.
2. After 5 minutes, combine pairs into groups of four. Each student shares their partner's responses, and the group compiles a complete tally for their four members.
3. Select three groups (e.g., Auni & Gan, Fatim & Hadwin, Afif & Dhivenassh) to present their tally chart to the class, speaking in full sentences: 'In our group, the most popular hobby is... because...'
4. As a class, compile the data into a master tally on the board, and discuss the overall favourite hobby in 1 Meekness.

 

Post-lesson

1. Students write two sentences in their journal: 'In my class, the most common hobby is ___ because ___.' and 'One new hobby I learned today is ___.'
2. Quick pair share: each student reads their sentences to a partner and receives one piece of feedback.
entries.reflection_html: Most students confidently used the target vocabulary during pair work, especially Auni and Gan who produced extended responses. Afif, however, needed minimal prompting to switch from Malay to English. The survey activity successfully encouraged critical thinking as Dhivenassh asked follow-up questions like 'Why do you like it?'.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show 4 images of unusual hobbies (extreme ironing, competitive eating, tree shaping, speed knitting) and ask 'What are these people doing?' to activate prior knowledge.
2. In pairs, students guess the hobby and share if they have heard of any such activity; AAYRA and DHIVENASSH lead sharing initial ideas.
3. Elicit the term 'unusual hobbies' and write on board, asking 'Why might someone choose an unusual hobby?' to spark curiosity.

 

Lesson Development

Vocabulary Input

1. Introduce key phrases: 'quirk', 'passion project', 'offbeat', 'niche community' and write definitions on the board.
2. Model pronunciation and ask CHOYE KAI EN and HADWIN to repeat each phrase in a sentence.
3. Clarify that these words help describe unusual hobbies and will be used in the main activity.

 

Jigsaw Discussion: Unusual Hobby Cards

1. Divide class into 3 groups: Group A (AAYRA, AFIF IRSYADUDDIN, AHMAD HARRAZ, AUNI), Group B (CHOYE KAI EN, DHIVENASSH, FATIN AQILAH), Group C (FATIN NURZAFIRAH, GAN KOK XIAN, HADWIN).
2. Give each group a short text about a different unusual hobby: Group A – 'Extreme Ironing', Group B – 'Competitive Eating', Group C – 'Tree Shaping' (each text is 4-5 sentences describing the hobby, its history, and why people do it).
3. Groups read and discuss key points: what the hobby is, why it is unusual, and one reason people enjoy it.
4. Remix into new trios (each trio has one member from A, B, C): e.g., AAYRA, CHOYE KAI EN, GAN KOK XIAN; AFIF, DHIVENASSH, FATIN NURZAFIRAH; AHMAD HARRAZ, FATIN AQILAH, HADWIN.
5. In trios, each student explains their hobby using target vocabulary ('This quirk hobby started in...', 'It attracts a niche community...'), others ask one question each.
6. Teacher monitors and prompts stronger students (e.g., AUNI, HADWIN) to extend answers with connectors like 'furthermore', 'in contrast'.

 

Feedback and Peer Evaluation

1. Bring class together; ask FATIN AQILAH to share one interesting fact from a trio discussion.
2. Highlight good use of target vocabulary and complex sentences by students like AFIF IRSYADUDDIN and GAN KOK XIAN.
3. Briefly explain that speaking includes both fluency and accuracy – encourage risk-taking with new words.

 

Mini Presentation: My Unusual Hobby Idea

1. In pairs (e.g., AAYRA & FATIN NURZAFIRAH, AFIF & CHOYE KAI EN, AHMAD HARRAZ & DHIVENASSH, AUNI & GAN KOK XIAN, FATIN AQILAH & HADWIN), each student invents a new unusual hobby and prepares a 30-second pitch using the vocabulary.
2. Teacher gives 3 minutes for preparation; encourages pair feedback on use of target phrases.
3. Four volunteers (selected by teacher: HADWIN, AAYRA, FATIN AQILAH, GAN KOK XIAN) present their hobby to the class; audience votes for the most creative hobby using thumbs up/down.

 

Post-lesson

1. Students write one sentence in their journal: 'The most interesting hobby I learned about today is ______ because ______.'
2. Pair up with a different partner and share one sentence orally; teacher circulates to listen for target vocabulary.
3. Exit ticket: on a sticky note, write one new word/phrase learned and one question they still have about unusual hobbies.
entries.reflection_html: Most students engaged well with the jigsaw activity; HADWIN and AUNI demonstrated strong critical thinking by linking vocabulary to their invented hobbies. AAYRA and FATIN AQILAH showed good fluency in presentations, while AFIF IRSYADUDDIN and GAN KOK XIAN used complex connectors effectively. For future lessons, I can include more structured peer feedback forms to deepen analysis.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a short video clip of people enjoying various hobbies (e.g., painting, cycling, reading) to activate prior knowledge.
2. Ask students: 'What is your favourite hobby? Why do you like it?' and elicit a few responses from Auni, Choye Kai En, and Gan Kok Xian.
3. Introduce the lesson objective: to write a paragraph about their favourite hobby with reasons, then present it to the class.

 

Lesson Development

Model Text Analysis

1. Display a model paragraph: 'My favourite hobby is reading because it transports me to different worlds and improves my vocabulary. I spend at least an hour reading every day before bed. It also helps me relax after a long day at school.'
2. Point out the structure: topic sentence (hobby + opinion), reason 1 with supporting detail, reason 2, and a concluding statement.
3. Highlight connectors: 'because', 'also', 'after' as cohesive devices.

 

Brainstorming and Drafting

1. Ask students to choose their favourite hobby and write down two reasons why they enjoy it, using a simple graphic organizer (hobby in centre, reasons in surrounding circles).
2. Instruct each student to write a first draft of a paragraph on their own, following the model structure. Teacher circulates to support weaker students like Dhivenassh and Hadwin.
3. Pair up students (e.g., Afif with Fatin Aqilah, Ahmad Harraz with Fatin Nurzafirah) to read each other's drafts and give one suggestion for improvement (e.g., add a connector or more detail).

 

Peer Feedback and Revision

1. Explain that peer feedback should be constructive: point out one good thing and one area to improve.
2. Demonstrate with an example draft: 'Good reason, but you could add a second reason or a concluding sentence.'
3. Remind students to revise their drafts based on feedback, focusing on clarity and use of connectors.

 

Final Writing and Presentation

1. Give students 10 minutes to write their final version neatly on a clean sheet of paper.
2. Select three volunteers (e.g., Aayra Faiz, Choye Kai En, Gan Kok Xian) to present their paragraph to the class, reading aloud with expression.
3. Collect all final paragraphs for assessment.

 

Post-lesson

1. Ask students to reflect on one new thing they learned about a classmate's hobby from the presentations.
2. Summarise the key points: a good paragraph has a clear topic, reasons with details, and connectors.
3. Assign optional homework: write a short paragraph about a hobby they want to try in the future.
entries.reflection_html: Today's lesson engaged stronger students like Aayra Faiz and Choye Kai En, who produced well-structured paragraphs with clear reasons. Afif Irsyaduddin needed minimal support with connectors, showing progress. The peer feedback activity fostered collaboration and critical thinking as students like Auni and Dhivenassh gave constructive suggestions.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of a food market and ask students to name any food they see.
2. Play a short video of a food song and have students clap when they hear a food word.
3. Elicit favourite foods from Adriesya and Indah using the question 'What food do you like?'.

 

Lesson Development

Food Vocabulary and Sentence Frames

1. Introduce 10 food words (rice, noodles, chicken, fish, eggs, bread, milk, fruit, vegetables, cake) using flashcards with pictures.
2. Model the sentence frames 'I like ___' and 'I don't like ___' on the board, pointing to the food cards.
3. Choral repetition of the vocabulary and frames with the whole class, then individual practice with Izz Rayyan and Izzara.

 

Pair Speaking Practice

1. Each student receives a worksheet with a table of food pictures and blank columns for 'like' and 'don't like'.
2. In pairs (e.g., Mohamad Hazim and Mohammad Izz Muqri), students ask each other 'Do you like (food)?' and tick the correct column based on their partner's answer.
3. Teacher circulates to support weaker students like Mohd Aidil and Muhammad Adeeb, prompting with the sentence frames if needed.
4. After 10 minutes, selected pairs (e.g., Muhammad Aiman and Muhammad Amirul) demonstrate their conversation in front of the class.

 

Post-lesson

1. Quick recap: teacher holds up food cards and students shout 'like' or 'don't like' as a class.
2. Students write one sentence about their favourite food on a sticky note and paste it on the board.
entries.reflection_html: Students were engaged during the set induction, especially Adriesya who eagerly named several foods. During the pair activity, Indah and Izz Rayyan used the sentence frames correctly with minimal prompting. A few weaker students like Mohd Aidil needed extra guidance but improved by the end. Overall, the class successfully practised speaking about likes and dislikes using simple vocabulary.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of a simple menu board with 5 food/drink items (rice, noodles, chicken, juice, water) and ask 'What do you see?'
2. Ask students to point to their favourite item and say 'I like...' using a word bank provided on the board.
3. Introduce the lesson: 'Today we will read a menu and order food like in a restaurant.'

 

Lesson Development

Reading a Menu

1. Distribute a simplified menu with 4 categories: Main Dishes (Nasi Lemak - RM3, Fried Rice - RM4), Drinks (Teh Tarik - RM2, Orange Juice - RM3), Snacks (Curry Puff - RM1, Samosa - RM1), Desserts (Ice Cream - RM2, Cendol - RM3).
2. Model reading aloud the menu items and prices, pointing to each word and using gestures for clarity.
3. Highlight key phrases: 'I would like...', 'How much is...?', 'Can I have...?' and write them on the board with translations.

 

Ordering Role Play

1. Pair students (e.g., Adriesya with Indah, Izz Rayyan with Izzara) and give each pair a simple order card with 2-3 items (e.g., 'Nasi Lemak, Teh Tarik').
2. One student plays 'customer' and the other 'waiter'. The customer uses a sentence frame: 'I would like [item]' and asks 'How much is [item]?'. The waiter reads the menu and answers. The customer then says 'Okay, I'll take it.'
3. After 3 minutes, swap roles. Monitor and help weaker pairs by whispering prompts. Extension: Let a pair perform in front of the class for encouragement.

 

Post-lesson

1. Each student writes 2 sentences on a worksheet: 'I would like ______. It is RM_____.' using their chosen items from the menu.
2. Collect worksheets for informal assessment. Praise effort and recap key phrases.
entries.reflection_html: Adriesya and Indah successfully used sentence frames with minimal prompting. Izz Rayyan struggled with price reading but improved after peer help from Izzara. Mohamad Hazim Daniel and Mohd Aidil Fitri needed extra support but completed the role play with a word bank. Overall, guided repetition helped comprehension.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of nasi lemak on the screen and ask students to name the food.
2. Ask students to share their favourite Malaysian food using the sentence frame: 'My favourite food is ______.'
3. Write three student responses on the board (e.g., from Adriesya, Indah, and Izz Rayyan) as examples.

 

Lesson Development

Parts of a Paragraph

1. Explain that a paragraph has a topic sentence (what you like), supporting details (why/how), and a closing sentence (sum up).
2. Show an example paragraph: 'My favourite food is nasi lemak. It is tasty and spicy. I eat it for breakfast. I love nasi lemak.'
3. Point out the topic sentence (first), details (second and third), and closing (last).

 

Guided Writing - My Favourite Food

1. Give each student a worksheet with sentence starters: 'My favourite food is...', 'It is...', 'I like it because...', 'I eat it for...', 'I love...' and a word bank (e.g., delicious, hot, sweet, sour, breakfast, lunch, dinner).
2. Ask students to write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about their favourite food using the starters and word bank. Circulate and help weaker students like Mohamad Hazim and Muhammad Adeeb.
3. Pair students to read their paragraphs to each other. Encourage pairs like Izzara and Mohd Aidil Fitri to give one compliment.

 

Post-lesson

1. Ask 2-3 volunteers (e.g., Muhammad Aiman Rayyan and Muhammad Amirul Qayyum) to read their paragraphs aloud.
2. Give praise for good vocabulary use (e.g., 'delicious' from Indah) and correct common errors on the board (e.g., 'I likes' -> 'I like').
entries.reflection_html: Students were engaged during the picture activity. Adriesya and Izz Rayyan confidently shared their favourite food. Most students, including Mohamad Hazim and Muhammad Adeeb, completed their paragraphs with help from the word bank and guidance.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a picture of a person sneezing with a thermometer in mouth and ask 'What's wrong with him?'
2. Elicit responses like 'He has a fever' or 'He is sick' and write key words on board.
3. Ask 'Have you ever given advice to a sick friend? What did you say?' to activate prior knowledge.

 

Lesson Development

Health Vocabulary Input

1. Present 8 health problems (cough, fever, headache, stomachache, cold, flu, sore throat, toothache) with images and pronunciation.
2. Introduce common advice structures: 'You should...', 'You shouldn't...', 'If I were you, I would...'
3. Model a short dialogue: 'What's wrong? I have a headache. You should rest and drink water.'

 

Pair Advice Speaking

1. In pairs, Student A draws a problem card (e.g., 'You have a stomachache') and Student B gives two pieces of advice using target language.
2. After 2 minutes, swap roles with a new card (8 cards total: cough, fever, headache, stomachache, cold, flu, sore throat, toothache).
3. Teacher monitors and notes good examples; then selects Devesh and Khaïsara to demonstrate their dialogue to class.

 

Comparison and Justification

1. Pose a challenge: 'Which health problem is the worst? Give two reasons.'
2. In pairs, students discuss and prepare a short opinion (e.g., 'Flu is the worst because you feel tired and can't go to school.')
3. Ask Aqilah and Azwa to share their opinion; encourage others to agree or disagree politely.

 

Post-lesson

1. Quick recall game: Teacher says a symptom, students shout the advice.
2. Exit ticket: Each student writes one new health word and one advice sentence they learned today.
3. Assign homework: Prepare a 1-minute health advice talk for a friend (record audio).
entries.reflection_html: Today's lesson went well with active participation. Devesh used advanced language to compare flu and cold, and Aqilah confidently gave reasons for her opinion. The pair speaking activity allowed all students to practise, though a few needed prompting to use the new structures.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. In pairs, brainstorm three healthy habits you already practice and write them down.
2. Share one habit from your pair with the class, and I'll list them on the board.
3. Today we’ll read about healthy habits and discuss which ones are most important for us.

 

Lesson Development

Key Vocabulary for Healthy Habits

1. I'll show three key terms: 'balanced diet', 'hydration', and 'sleep hygiene'.
2. In pairs, define each term in your own words and give an example.
3. We’ll review definitions together, clarifying any confusion.

 

Read and Respond: Healthy Habits Text

1. Read the 150-word passage about three healthy habits: eating well, staying active, and getting enough sleep.
2. Answer five open-ended comprehension questions individually (e.g., 'Why is hydration important?').
3. Compare your answers with a partner, then we discuss as a class.

 

Pair Discussion: Which Habit Matters Most?

1. In pairs, decide which of the three habits from the text is most important for teenagers.
2. Prepare two reasons to support your choice.
3. Share your opinion with another pair; we'll conclude with a class vote.

 

Post-lesson

1. Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) describing one healthy habit you will start or improve this week.
2. Hand in your paragraph as an exit ticket before you leave.
entries.reflection_html: Devesh and Fawwaz showed deep analysis during the pair discussion, comparing habits critically. Azwa Shahirah contributed a unique perspective on sleep hygiene, which sparked a lively debate.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a sample mini poster titled '5 Tips for Better Sleep' and ask students what they notice about the layout and language.
2. Elicit from students: 'What health tips do you already know or follow?' and write a few on the board.
3. Explain that today they will create their own mini poster with health tips for other teenagers.

 

Lesson Development

Structure of a Mini Poster

1. A mini poster needs a catchy title, 3-5 tips written as short imperative sentences (e.g., 'Drink more water.'), and simple visuals or icons.
2. The language should be clear, persuasive, and aimed at their peers; use phrases like 'You should...' or 'Try to...'.
3. Show a second example on screen and highlight the use of bullet points and color to make tips stand out.

 

Drafting and Creating Health Tips Mini Poster

1. In pairs (e.g., Ahmad Amsyar & Aliff Fahmii, Aqilah & Areej, Azwa & Devesh, Fawwaz & Hani, Khaïsara & Leong), brainstorm 3-5 health tips on a chosen aspect (e.g., mental health, exercise, diet).
2. Write a draft of the poster on A4 paper with a title, tips, and simple drawings—no need for perfection, focus on clear writing.
3. Conduct a 'Gallery Walk': each pair leaves their poster on the desk and walks around to read others' posters, leaving one positive comment on a sticky note.

 

Post-lesson

1. Collect the posters for teacher assessment on content (relevance, clarity) and language (imperatives, punctuation).
2. Ask students to write one sentence in their journal: 'What is one health tip I learned from a classmate’s poster?'
3. Briefly share two strong examples from Azwa Shahirah and Leong Kah Kin to highlight good use of imperatives and catchy titles.
entries.reflection_html: Today’s activity showed strong engagement from all pairs. Hani Raihannah and Khaïsara Irdina created very clear, well-structured posters with imperative sentences. Azwa Shahirah and Devesh impressed with creative visuals that supported their tips. The class demonstrated good understanding of writing for a specific audience, and the peer feedback helped reinforce correct language use.
